claims.claim: Athanasius of Alexandria was Bishop of Alexandria and Patriarch of Alexandria, born c. 296–298 and died 2 May 373.
The Tomus ad Antiochenos was written in 362 on behalf of a regional synod that Athanasius convened in Alexandria in the spring or summer of that year.
The work was addressed to a five-member commission of fellow bishops: Eusebius, Lucifer, Asterius, Kymatius, and Anatolius, who were working to resolve the schism in Antioch.
The letter was written to mediate the schism between 'Eustathians' and 'Meletians' in the parishes of Antioch, specifically to achieve theological agreement based on the Nicene Creed.

The occasion was prompted by the recall of exiled bishops after the accession of the emperor Julian in November 361 and his edict of February 362, with many formerly separated Christians now wishing for peace and many severing connection with the Arians.

The Tomus required those seeking communion to anathematize the Arian heresy, confess the Nicene faith, and anathematize those who say the Holy Spirit is a creature and separate from the Essence of Christ.

The work survives through manuscript tradition and is preserved in collections of Athanasius's writings, including Greek original texts and English translations in patristic collections such as the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series.

The Tomus played a key role in Trinitarian theological debates between the one-hypostasis and three-hypostasis models of the Trinity, anticipating the turning point from the 370s onward and paving the way for the theological language of the three Cappadocians (Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus).

The work matters because it recognized that certain theological points of contention were based not only on differences of belief but also on different language rules or conceptual differences between Latin and Greek, helping establish the concept of one being (ousia) and three hypostases that became binding at the First Council of Constantinople in 381.
